reasons: Mostly definitions and small helpers, and no tests are visible in this packet.
Missing values are handled by returning null.

terms.meaning: A label describing the shape of a piece of data, so mistakes are caught early.
A named type listing the fields an object must have.
A value that comes with its source link and a note.
A deliberate empty value meaning the figure is not known.
A small reusable function that does one job.
The code reads values but never changes them.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Shared types and imports
sections.what: Brings in the evidence field type from the shared display component and the source reference type from the shared API client, and passes the evidence field type on for other files.
sections.why: Keeps evidence display in one shared place, so this file does not depend on scan-specific code.
sections.watch_out: The source reference import reaches up to the repository root, so moving either folder breaks it.

sections.name: ScanCapacity
sections.title: Capacity figure
sections.what: Describes a capacity figure with a value and a unit, and either can be empty.
sections.why: Gives capacity a simple shape, separate from the evidence-based fields.
sections.watch_out: Capacity has no source link fields, so it is the one figure here that carries no evidence.

sections.name: ScanProject
sections.title: One project record
sections.what: Describes one project: its name, industry, cost fields, schedule fields, reason fields, status, location and site type. Each figure is an evidence field or empty, and the schedule also records whether its slip is approximate and why.
sections.why: This is the full set of values the benchmark slides read for each project.
sections.watch_out: The approximate flag must be checked before showing a schedule slip as exact.

sections.name: ScanResponse
sections.title: List response
sections.what: Describes the response that lists projects: the industry name, a count, and the list of projects.
sections.why: The response is what the benchmark pages receive from the server.
sections.watch_out: Nothing here checks that the count equals the number of projects in the list.

sections.name: SynthesisBullet
sections.title: One synthesis bullet
sections.what: Describes one AI statement: the project name, the statement text, and optional source references.
sections.why: Each statement names its project so a reader can check it against the data.
sections.watch_out: Projects are matched by name, not by id, so a name mismatch breaks the link.

sections.name: SynthesisCategory
sections.title: Synthesis category
sections.what: Describes a themed group: a category name and its list of bullets.
sections.why: Groups related statements under one heading.

sections.name: ScanSynthesis
sections.title: Whole synthesis answer
sections.what: Describes the full AI answer: a title, the wrong-side categories, the right-side categories, and two straplines.
sections.why: Matches the structure the synthesis slide displays.
sections.watch_out: The text comes from the AI model and nothing here checks it.

sections.name: SynthesisResponse
sections.title: Synthesis response states
sections.what: Describes the server answer as one of three states: ok with a synthesis, not configured, or error with a message.
sections.why: Lets the screen handle each state separately.
sections.watch_out: A new state name not listed here would fall through to the idle display.

sections.name: fieldNum
sections.title: Read a number from an evidence field
sections.what: Returns the field's value as a number, or empty when the value is missing, blank or not a number.
sections.why: Lets calculations ignore missing figures instead of failing.
sections.watch_out: Values with thousands separators, such as 1,200, do not parse and become empty.

sections.name: fieldStr, MONTHS
sections.title: Read text from an evidence field and month names
sections.what: Returns the field's value as text, or empty when missing. Also defines the three-letter month names used for display.
sections.why: Lets the screen show text safely, and keeps month names in one place.
sections.watch_out: The month names are used only for date display.

sections.name: parseISODate
sections.title: Read a date from text
sections.what: Looks for a year, month and day at the start of the text and returns them as numbers, or empty if the pattern is not found.
sections.why: Dates in the data are stored as text, so this pulls out the parts for comparison.
sections.watch_out: Only dates starting with year, month, day are recognised. Other formats return empty.

sections.name: fmtMonthYear
sections.title: Show a date as month and year
sections.what: Turns a date into a short month and year, such as Jan 2024. Text that is not a date is shown as it is.
sections.why: Gives a readable date while keeping any free-text entry visible.
sections.watch_out: Free text can appear in a date column without warning.

sections.name: fmtMillions
sections.title: Format money in millions
sections.what: Rounds a figure to one decimal and adds thousands separators, for example 1462 becomes 1,462.
sections.why: Gives every budget the same readable format.
sections.watch_out: The code assumes figures are already in millions. If a source sends raw dollars, figures will display far too large.

sections.name: budgetOverran
sections.title: Budget overrun check
sections.what: Returns true only when both a planned and an actual budget exist and the actual figure is higher.
sections.why: Flags projects that spent more than planned.
sections.watch_out: A missing planned or actual figure counts as not over budget, which can hide real overruns.

sections.name: scheduleOverran
sections.title: Schedule overrun check
sections.what: Returns true if the recorded schedule slip is above zero. Otherwise it compares the planned end date with the actual end date.
sections.why: Flags projects that finished later than planned, using whichever figure is available.
sections.watch_out: The date comparison orders dates correctly but is not a true day count, so do not use it to measure how late a project is.

summary: Describes the shape of the benchmark project data that the front end receives, plus small helpers that read values safely.
purpose: Gives the front end one shared description of project data, synthesis answers, and formatting helpers.
why: The header comment says this mirrors the server's data shape, is read only, and keeps missing values as null rather than inventing them.
how: 1. Declares the shapes of a project, its capacity, the list response, and the synthesis answer. 2. Provides helpers that read numbers and text from evidence fields safely. 3. Provides date and money formatting. 4. Provides checks for budget overrun and schedule overrun.
inputs: Project data returned by the server, including evidence fields that carry a value and its source.
outputs: Typed structures for the rest of the app, formatted text, numbers or null, and true or false overrun flags.
risks: Nothing here checks that the server really sends these shapes, so a mismatch shows up as blank or wrong values. Overrun checks skip projects with missing numbers, so they can look on budget when data is missing. The schedule check compares dates with a simple formula that orders them correctly but is not a real day count. The import reaches up to a shared folder outside this component area, so moving folders breaks it.
debug: If values look blank, compare the server response with these shapes and check the helper that reads that field. If overrun flags look wrong, check the planned and actual figures on that project.
